The story behind an idea

Triplett's cyclists and social facilitation

In 1898, a cycling-loving psychologist noticed that people rode faster in company.

Norman Triplett, at Indiana University, looked at cycling race records and noticed that riders were faster when racing against others or behind a pacer than when riding alone against the clock.

One of the first social experiments

To test it under controlled conditions, he asked children to wind fishing line onto a reel as fast as possible, alone or alongside another child. Many were faster in company. His 1898 study is often called the first social psychology experiment, although the data were modest.

In 1965, Robert Zajonc refined the effect: the presence of others improves performance on easy or well-practised tasks but worsens it on difficult or new ones. That is why an elite athlete shines in front of a crowd while a beginner freezes.

References

  1. Triplett, N. (1898). The dynamogenic factors in pacemaking and competition. American Journal of Psychology, 9(4), 507–533.
  2. Zajonc, R. B. (1965). Social facilitation. Science, 149(3681), 269–274.
